cards.text: Friend, the Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), has spent a while watching people chase the wind (Ecclesiastes 4:16). Now he walks us up to the house of God, and the first thing he tells us at the door is to guard our steps. Walk in slow, friend, like the new hire on day one who hasn't figured out who's in charge yet.

cards.question: At the house of God, the Teacher says to draw near to ___ rather than to offer the sacrifice of fools.
The Teacher says the fools who offer the sacrifice of fools at the house of God know they are doing wrong.

cards.text: Next he goes after the mouth: don't be quick to speak, and don't be hasty in your heart to utter a word before God. Friend, that's me answering the group chat before I finish READING it, FIVE replies deep in the WRONG conversation.

cards.question: The Teacher says to let your words be few before God. What reason does he give?

answers.text: God is in heaven and you are on earth
God already knows what you will say
God listens best to quiet hearts

cards.text: Then he paints a picture: as a dream comes through many cares. You know the one, friend, that stressed-out week when you dream your boss is a goose running the Monday meeting.

cards.question: In the Teacher's picture, a dream comes through many cares. Whose speech does he say comes with many words?

cards.text: Now the Teacher turns to vows made to God. I promised my oven a clean rack back in March, friend, and that oven has NOT forgotten.

cards.question: The Teacher says that once you make a vow to God, you can take your time fulfilling it.
Don't delay in fulfilling a vow, the Teacher says, because God takes no pleasure in ___.
What does the Teacher say is better than making a vow to God and not fulfilling it?

answers.text: Not making a vow at all
Letting a priest vow for you

cards.text: Then comes the warning: don't let your mouth cause your flesh to sin. My mouth once bragged I could carry SIX trays at once, friend, and it was NOT my mouth that landed face-down in the chocolate chips.

cards.question: The Teacher says not to tell the messenger that your vow was a ___.
If your words make God angry, what does the Teacher say could happen to the work of your hands?

answers.text: Others could take credit for it

cards.text: He brings the dream picture back one last time: as many dreams bring futility, so do many words. Like that goose-boss dream, friend, a big pile of words goes NOWHERE.

cards.question: After all those warnings about words and vows, what does the Teacher tell us to do?

findings.problem: The stop repeatedly pauses just before an unseen detail or the unseen second half of a verse. Cards 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 13 and 14 do not provide enough earlier context to reason out the stated answer over the alternatives. For example, card 4 supplies none of the three proposed reasons in card 5. Only cards 9, 11 and 16 are clearly informed guesses, so the discovery questions are not limited to a few.

rule.text: A few discovery questions are fine. Some moments can't be reasoned out, like where Jonah's ship is headed. A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

findings.problem: Card 1 covers guarding my steps but gives no setup for the contrast between listening and offering the sacrifice of fools. Filling in 'listen' therefore asks for unseen wording rather than testing a meaning the baker can reason out.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: Neither the vow transition in card 8 nor the delay question in card 9 sets up God's stated reason for not delaying. The baker is asked to complete the line with 'fools' without a basis for reasoning out that reason; the earlier mention of fools in verse 1 does not supply it.

findings.problem: Card 12 mentions only the mouth causing the flesh to sin. It does not set up the messenger or an attempt to excuse the vow, so filling in 'mistake' requires guessing the unseen wording of the next line.
